story: Venus is a hellish world where temperatures are hot enough to melt lead, surface pressure is 90 times that of Earth, and the sky is choked with sulfuric acid. Yet, scientists suspect it once harbored vast oceans. To uncover the truth, NASA is returning to Venus with DAVINCI, its first atmospheric entry probe since the 1970s. Set to launch in the late 2020s, DAVINCI will release a beach-ball-sized titanium sphere directly into the toxic, crushing air. For about an hour, this highly engineered sphere will plunge through the clouds, sniffing noble gases and trace elements to trace Venus's climate evolution. Before its final crash-landing, the probe will capture the first high-resolution views of Venus's rugged tesserae mountains since 1982. This daring mission, named after Leonardo da Vinci, could rewrite the history of Earth's mysterious twin.
angle: NASA is dropping a beach-ball-sized titanium sphere into Venus's lead-melting, acidic, high-pressure atmosphere to sniff out the planet's lost oceans.

claims.claim: Venus is comparable in size to Earth but features a surface hot enough to melt lead.
Venus's atmosphere has a surface pressure over 90 times that of Earth's sea level.
Venus is surrounded by highly corrosive clouds of sulfuric acid.
NASA's DAVINCI mission was selected in June 2021 to explore Venus.
DAVINCI stands for Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging.
The mission belongs to NASA's low-cost Discovery Program.
DAVINCI was originally proposed in 2015 but was defeated in 2017 by the Lucy and Psyche missions.
The mission's name was temporarily modified to 'DAVINCI+' before being reverted back to 'DAVINCI'.
The mission's principal investigator is James B. Garvin of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center.
NASA selected another Venus mission, VERITAS, to launch around the same time as DAVINCI.
The DAVINCI mission will feature a descent probe shaped like a sphere.
The spherical probe's descent through the Venusian atmosphere will last approximately one hour.
DAVINCI's probe will be the first spacecraft to perform in situ atmospheric measurements of Venus since the Soviet Vega missions in 1985.
The spacecraft will perform two flybys of Venus prior to deploying the descent probe.
DAVINCI's acronym is a tribute to Leonardo da Vinci.
The descent probe will capture images of Venus's rugged, ridged terrain known as 'tesserae'.
The probe will measure noble gases to help scientists understand the origin and evolution of the Venusian atmosphere.
One of the descent probe's main instruments is the Venus Mass Spectrometer (VMS).
The Venus Tunable Laser Spectrometer (VTLS) instrument will be provided by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
The mission aims to investigate whether Venus once had water oceans.

disputed: The initial proposal in 2015 named Lori Glaze as the Principal Investigator, but by selection in 2021, James B. Garvin was named PI; the script should attribute the initial leadership to Glaze and the active mission to Garvin.

Early proposals estimated a launch by 2021 and a 63-minute descent, whereas final 2021 plans target late 2020s and generalize the descent to about an hour; the script should use the updated late 2020s timeframe and say about an hour.
